input.content:
The fastest way to fix a bug is to write the failing test first.

It feels backwards. You already know what's broken, why slow down to reproduce it in code? Because the test is the only proof the fix actually works, and the only guardrail against the bug crawling back six months from now.

Three takeaways from doing this every day:

1. Reproducing the bug in a test forces you to understand it. Half the "fixes" I've watched fail were patches to a symptom nobody had isolated.

2. A red test turning green is honest feedback. "It works on my machine" is not.

3. The test outlives the fix. Refactors, dependency bumps, teammates in a hurry — the test keeps catching the same regression forever.

The extra ten minutes up front saves the hour of firefighting when it silently comes back in production.

What's the last bug you shipped a fix for without writing a test — and would you do it that way again?
